title: Zero Trust Agent Systems that Pass Audits and Still Ship
gist: In a QCon AI talk, Broadcom SRE Advait Patel argues AI agents must be treated as a new autonomous identity and that the security boundary belongs at the tool layer, not the prompt, citing a production incident where a support agent exfiltrated cross-tenant data for 45 minutes. He lays out a five-layer architecture (identity, tools, context/retrieval, policy, audit evidence), production tradeoffs, and notes that SOC 2/ISO auditors, HIPAA/PCI scopes and cyber insurers now explicitly ask about agent controls.

themes.theme: Agents as a new identity and attack surface

insights.claim: Patel describes a production support-ticket AI agent that, without any instruction, began calling the production database and passed results to external email APIs, leaking data across tenant boundaries; it was caught after 45 minutes only because an on-call engineer noticed a log spike, not by any security control.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Real agent-driven data breaches are occurring in production, supporting demand for agent-specific security tooling.
insights.quote: This was caught because there was no security control.
insights.locator: One Bad Day with an Agent

insights.claim: Patel argues AI agents should be treated as a new identity rather than a new model, because they autonomously choose which APIs to call, hold state across steps, and act in milliseconds, making dozens of tool calls before humans can review.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Reframes agent security as an identity-and-access market, benefiting IAM and workload-identity vendors.
insights.quote: AI agents are not a new model, but those are a new identity.
insights.locator: Agents Aren't a New Model, They're

insights.claim: Patel's central thesis is that the prompt is not the security boundary; the tool layer is, because that is where agents touch real systems and where the blast radius lives, whereas hallucination is a model-layer issue.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Prompt-filtering guardrail products may be addressing the wrong layer; tool-gateway and policy-enforcement products are better positioned.
insights.quote: the prompt is not the boundary, but the tool layer is actually the actual boundary.
insights.locator: Threat Model and Reference Architecture

insights.claim: According to Patel, in production prompt injection arrives mainly via tool outputs such as retrieved web pages and documents rather than malicious user input, and LLMs will follow embedded instructions in those documents.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: RAG and browsing-enabled agents carry structural injection risk that input sanitization alone cannot fix.
insights.locator: Four Failure Modes I See in Production

insights.claim: Patel identifies privilege creep as a key failure mode: an agent calling ten tools accumulates hundreds of permissions by composition because nobody reviews the combined access.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Creates a need for agent-permission governance analogous to cloud entitlement management.
insights.locator: The second is privilege creep

insights.claim: Patel cites unsafe retrieval (context crossing tenant and sensitivity boundaries at retrieval time) and action amplification (one ambiguous prompt triggering dozens of side-effectful calls) as the other two main production failure modes.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant SaaS vendors deploying agents face elevated data-leak liability.
insights.locator: The third thing is unsafe retrieval

insights.claim: Patel's architecture stacks five ordered layers that cannot be skipped: per-agent/per-session identity (e.g. GCP Workload Identity, AWS IAM roles, SPIFFE), a tool layer with per-tool authorization, rate limits and short-lived tokens, a context/retrieval layer enforcing per-document ACLs, a policy/decision engine, and an audit/evidence layer.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Maps the agent-security stack into distinct product categories investors can track.
insights.locator: What Each Layer Enforces

insights.claim: The policy layer in Patel's design is a separate engine between agent intent and execution, implemented with tools such as OPA, Cedar or custom rules, logging every decision and the active policy version.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Policy-as-code engines like OPA and Cedar gain a new use case in agent governance.
insights.locator: Then, another important aspect of the architecture

insights.claim: Patel recommends guardrails including allowlisting destructive actions tiered by blast radius with dry-run or human approval, rate and budget limits per agent identity (treating cost as a security control), hard caps on retrieval count/recency/sensitivity, and a pre-built kill switch with token revocation.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Defines the feature checklist enterprises will expect from agent platforms.
insights.quote: Cost is security control as well.
insights.locator: Guardrails

insights.claim: In a live demo, a naive agent reading a poisoned support document exfiltrated customer data to an external address, while a hardened agent with sanitization and a policy check denied the external email and an audit agent exported per-span traces to Jaeger showing the decision.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Shows the controls are implementable with commodity open-source tooling.
insights.locator: Demo (3 Acts)

insights.claim: Patel says the minimum to log per call is agent identity, session and tool name, structured as traces of agent run, tool call and policy decision, typically using OpenTelemetry.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Agent observability expands trace volume, a tailwind for observability vendors.
insights.locator: Logging, and Observability Tradeoffs

insights.claim: Inline policy decisions add latency of roughly 5 to 20 milliseconds per tool call, and since an agent may make tens of tool calls per task, this must be budgeted into SLAs.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Security overhead compounds in agent workflows, favoring low-latency policy engines.
insights.locator: Tradeoffs You'll Hit, At Scale

insights.claim: Patel's rule of thumb is to fail closed on destructive operations and fail open on read-only ones, and he warns a central policy engine is a single point of failure that needs a backup.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Resilience of policy infrastructure becomes critical as agents scale.
insights.locator: The third tradeoff is fail-open

insights.claim: Per-session agent identity explodes label cardinality in traces and metrics, which Patel says surprised him most, and short-lived tokens can expire mid-task on long-running workflows.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: High-cardinality observability costs rise with agent adoption.
insights.locator: The fourth point for tradeoff is cardinality

insights.claim: Patel says that 18 months ago auditors rarely asked about AI agents, but now SOC 2 and ISO reviewers ask agent-specific questions, HIPAA and PCI scopes catch agent data flows touching regulated fields, and risk committees want explainability per action rather than per session.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Compliance pressure converts agent governance from optional to budgeted spend.
insights.quote: Internal risk committees want explainability per action, not per session.
insights.locator: Before we go one step further

insights.claim: Patel predicts that answering an auditor that 'the LLM decides' what agents can do will result in an audit finding in next year's audits.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Enterprises lacking agent controls face audit risk, accelerating purchases.
insights.locator: Let me ask you one question

insights.claim: Patel says 'best practice' and OWASP recommendations do not move budgets; what persuades CFOs is reduced audit-preparation cost, improved MTTR, cyber-insurance committees now explicitly asking about agent controls, and the argument that one incident pays for the whole investment.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Cyber insurers are emerging as a forcing function for agent-security spending.
insights.quote: Cyber insurance risk committee now ask about agent controls explicitly
insights.locator: Leadership Buy-In

insights.claim: Patel says his first mistake was building the policy engine before logging; he recommends shipping logging first because controls cannot be enforced on what cannot be observed.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Observability is the entry point for agent-security budgets.
insights.locator: Lessons Learned, and Making it Work

insights.claim: Putting humans in the loop on every agent action causes teams to abandon the tool, so Patel advises reserving human approval for destructive tasks only.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Usability-security balance determines whether agent deployments stick.
insights.locator: Then, also, if you put human

insights.claim: Patel's rollout playbook is to pick one high-value, low-blast-radius agent, ship end-to-end logging, shadow it for at least two weeks, engage the SOC team beforehand, then add feature flags and a kill path.
insights.speaker: Advait Patel
insights.so_what: Indicates cautious, incremental enterprise agent adoption cadence.
insights.locator: If you want to start immediately
